summary: Tonga is an archipelagic kingdom in the South Pacific and the only country in the Pacific never formally colonized; it remains a constitutional monarchy.

ranking.name: Wesleyan Methodism (Free Wesleyan Church of Tonga)
ranking.description: In 1826 Wesleyan missionaries established a mission station in Tonga; in 1831 the chief Taufa'ahau was baptized and took the name "George," and in 1845 he unified Tonga and became King George Tupou I, so Methodism became the religion of the royal house and the state. In 1875 he promulgated a constitution that declared the Sabbath inviolable. In 1924 Queen Salote brought about the merger of the churches into the "Free Wesleyan Church of Tonga," of which the king is still a member, and so it is the largest denomination.

ranking.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
ranking.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons) first sent missionaries to Tonga in 1891 and re-established the mission after 1916. Schools run by the church, such as Liahona High School, provide a good education and help believers go to Utah and Hawaii in the United States to study and work, attracting large numbers of families. Tonga has thus become one of the countries with the highest proportion of Mormons in the world.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Marist missionaries of the Catholic Church arrived in Tonga in 1842, when Tupou I was contending for power with other chiefs, and some chiefs opposed to the Wesleyan faction and their people converted to Catholicism. The Catholic Church has invested deeply in education and is still the third-largest denomination, with believers on all the main islands.

ranking.name: Free Church of Tonga
ranking.description: In 1885, with the support of King Tupou I, the former missionary Shirley Baker pushed the founding of the "Free Church of Tonga," separate from the jurisdiction of the Australian Methodists, stressing that the church should be run independently by Tongans. When Queen Salote pushed the merger of the two sides in 1924, some believers refused to join and continued to operate under the name Free Church of Tonga, forming today's independent denomination.

ranking.name: Church of Tonga
ranking.description: The Church of Tonga is a Methodist denomination that split off after the church merger dispute of the 1920s and is made up mainly of nobles and believers unwilling to accept the merger arrangements. It is close to the Free Wesleyan Church in doctrine and liturgy, and the differences stem mainly from historical noble factions and struggles over church leadership.

religion.background: The Tongans originally followed a Polynesian religion centered on ancestors, spirits and sacred kingship. In the early 19th century Wesleyan missionaries came to Tonga; in 1831 Taufa'ahau was baptized and in 1845 he unified the country and became King George Tupou I, and from then on Christianity was closely bound up with the monarchy. In the late 19th century the church split into several Methodist factions, and Catholicism and Mormonism were also introduced one after another. Today Tonga is an extremely devout Christian country; the constitution makes Sunday the Sabbath, and most commercial activity must stop.

language.official: Tongan and English are the official languages.

ranking.name: Tongan
ranking.description: Tongan belongs to the Polynesian branch of the Austronesian family and is the mother tongue of the Tongans. In the 19th century Wesleyan missionaries devised a Latin-script writing system for Tongan and translated the Bible. Because Tonga was never fully colonized and was only a British protected state from 1900 to 1970, the royal house and government have always used Tongan, so almost all citizens have Tongan as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: The influence of English comes from the period of the British protected state of 1900–1970 and from church school education; today English and Tongan are both official languages, used in secondary and higher education, government documents and international affairs. Because large numbers of Tongans have moved to New Zealand, Australia and the United States, English is increasingly important in overseas communities and among the younger generation, but very few people in the country have English as a mother tongue.

language.history: Tongan belongs to the Polynesian branch, is close to Samoan, Niuean and others, and gradually took shape after Austronesian peoples of the Lapita culture reached Tonga about three thousand years ago. Tongan has a complex system of honorifics, with different vocabulary for the king, nobles and commoners. In the 19th century missionaries devised a Latin-script writing system for Tongan and translated the Bible. During the British protected state English became one of the languages of education, and today Tongan and English are both official languages.

ranking.name: Lu pulu
ranking.description: Canned corned beef or mutton, onion and coconut milk are wrapped in taro leaves, then wrapped again in banana leaves or foil and baked in an earth oven, rich and tender.
ranking.history: Wrapping ingredients in taro leaves and baking them in an earth oven is an ancient Polynesian method, but canned corned beef is a food imported in large quantities from New Zealand and elsewhere only in the 20th century, and it quickly became one of Tongans' favorite meats. Lu pulu is a must at the family feast after Sunday church services and at festive banquets. The spread of imported canned meat is also linked to Tonga's recent problems of obesity and chronic disease and has become a focus of public health discussion.

ranking.name: Ota ika (raw fish in coconut milk)
ranking.description: Fresh raw fish is diced and cured in lemon or lime juice until white, then mixed with coconut milk, onion, tomato, cucumber and chili, light and slightly sour.
ranking.history: Austronesian peoples have been skilled at seafaring and fishing since ancient times, and eating raw sea fish is a long tradition of the Pacific islands. The method of "cooking" fish with citrus juice is related to changes in diet after Europeans introduced citrus fruits, and similar dishes exist in Samoa, Fiji and Tahiti. In Tonga, surrounded by sea, ota ika is one of the most popular dishes at everyday meals and Sunday gatherings.

ranking.name: Umu (earth oven roast)
ranking.description: A pit is dug in the ground and stones are heated in it; taro, sweet potato, pork, fish and lu pulu are wrapped in leaves and placed on the stones, then covered and slow-cooked for several hours.
ranking.history: Earth-oven cooking is a tradition brought by the ancestors of the Polynesians when they migrated across the sea; in the days before metal cookware, heated stones made it possible to cook large quantities of food at once. Tonga's Sabbath rules forbid work on Sunday, so many families prepare the earth oven early on Sunday morning and the whole family enjoys it together after church. At royal celebrations, weddings and funerals, the earth oven is an indispensable way of cooking.

ranking.name: Puaka tunu (roast suckling pig)
ranking.description: A whole suckling pig is slowly turned on a spit over charcoal until the skin is golden and crisp and the meat juicy, the most solemn main dish at a Tongan feast.
ranking.history: The Lapita-culture ancestors who reached Tonga about three thousand years ago brought pigs, and pigs have since been an important symbol of wealth and ritual in the Pacific islands. At Tonga's "katoanga" feasts, weddings, funerals and royal coronations, the number of roast pigs represents the status and goodwill of the host family, and large royal celebrations often prepare hundreds or thousands. It remains the most symbolic food for entertaining in Tongan society.

ranking.name: Talo (taro)
ranking.description: Taro is a starchy tuberous root that is soft in texture after being baked in an earth oven or boiled, and its young leaves can also be cooked with coconut milk and eaten.
ranking.history: Taro is one of the "canoe crops" that the Austronesian ancestors brought from Southeast Asia to the Pacific, and for thousands of years, together with yam and breadfruit, it has formed the staple of the Tongans. Tonga traditionally holds the annual "'inasi" first-fruits ceremony, offering the best of the harvest such as yams and taro to the king as a symbol of loyalty to the crown. Today taro is still the most common starchy food at family tables and earth-oven feasts.
